content: Parallel to the spectrum licensing updates, the regulatory environment governing number portability has also experienced significant foundational developments and recent prospective shifts. Between 2020 and 2024, number portability in South Africa—defined as the ability for consumers to switch their service provider while retaining their existing phone number—was governed by regulations set forth by ICASA as part of the Numbering Plan Regulations of 2016 [94] . These regulations provided a robust framework enabling full number portability between both fixed and mobile numbers, thereby facilitating customer choice and fostering heightened competition within the telecommunications sector [95] . Businesses and individual consumers alike benefited from the option to transfer geographic and non-geographic numbers, which included mobile numbers and Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) system integrations, ensuring minimal operational disruption during provider transitions. The established porting process typically involved necessary coordination between the losing and gaining service providers, requiring explicit customer authorization and meticulous documentation, and although it was designed to be streamlined, it reportedly took time and significant effort to complete [93] . Across the broader African continent, processes for mobile number portability were generally considered among the fastest globally, taking less than 24 hours in many instances, though these timeframes may have varied considerably based on country-specific implementations and localized technical constraints. South Africa's regulations during this historical period continued to promote number portability as a fundamental consumer right, thereby strengthening its telecommunications infrastructure and aligning the national market with global trends in user empowerment [93] . While the regulatory foundation for number portability was relatively stable, potential disparities in practical implementation across different service providers were likely encountered, representing a common challenge noted generally across various African telecommunications markets.
